title: The Heat and Diffusion Equations
objectives: Write the one-dimensional heat equation and explain the role of the diffusivity $\alpha$
Sketch the separation-of-variables solution on a finite rod and compute the decay rate of a given mode
State and use the maximum principle and the smoothing/irreversibility properties of the heat equation
Step an explicit finite-difference scheme by hand and check the stability condition $r = \alpha\Delta t/\Delta x^2 \le 1/2$
Identify the diffusion term of the Black-Scholes PDE and explain why its numerics mirror heat-equation methods
motivation: Drop a dye cube into still water and watch it blur into a smooth cloud: diffusion is nature's great smoothing machine, and the heat equation is its law. The same equation, after a change of variables, drives the Black-Scholes pricing PDE, the $\tfrac12\sigma^2 S^2 V_{SS}$ term is diffusion in disguise. Understanding how heat spreads, how its solutions decay mode by mode, and how to step the equation numerically is therefore direct preparation for derivative pricing.

blocks.md: For a thin insulated rod of material with diffusivity $\alpha > 0$, with temperature $u(x,t)$, the one-dimensional heat equation is

blocks.caption: $u_t = \alpha\, u_{xx}$ on $0 < x < L$, $t > 0$, plus an initial temperature profile and boundary conditions.

blocks.md: The equation encodes one physical idea: heat flows from hot to cold, so $u$ increases where the profile is locally *below* its neighbours' average ($u_{xx} > 0$) and decreases where it is above ($u_{xx} < 0$). The constant $\alpha$ (units $\text{m}^2/\text{s}$) sets the pace: copper's $\alpha \approx 1.11 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{m}^2/\text{s}$ spreads heat in minutes where stainless steel takes hours. The same PDE with $\alpha$ renamed describes chemical diffusion, population spreading and, with the right change of variables, option pricing.

blocks.text: Two structural properties you must know

blocks.md: **Smoothing and irreversibility.** Heat solutions instantly become infinitely smooth and sharpening features are erased: an initial jagged profile becomes a gentle hump within moments. Running the equation *backwards* would un-blur the dye, it is catastrophically ill-posed, amplifying every high-frequency wiggle. That is why pricing PDEs are solved *forward in calendar time but backward from expiry*, a direction we exploit rather than fight. **Maximum principle.** On a closed rod, the maximum temperature over all time occurs either at $t = 0$ or at the boundaries, the interior can never spontaneously exceed everything around it. For option prices the analogue bounds the premium by the payoff's extreme values.

Take a rod of length $L$ with ends held at zero temperature and try a product solution $u(x,t) = X(x)\,T(t)$. Substituting into $u_t = \alpha u_{xx}$ and dividing by $\alpha X T$ separates the variables: each side must equal a constant $-\lambda$. The spatial problem $X'' = -\lambda X$ with $X(0) = X(L) = 0$ has solutions $X_n = \sin(n\pi x/L)$ for $\lambda_n = (n\pi/L)^2$, and each carries its own exponential clock:

blocks.caption: Initial shape decomposed into sine modes; high-frequency modes (large $n$) decay fastest, hence the instant smoothing.

blocks.title: Worked example: one mode on a unit rod
items: Take $L = 1$, $\alpha = 1$, initial profile $u(x,0) = \sin(\pi x)$ - a pure fundamental mode, so only $B_1 = 1$ survives.
Amplitude at $t = 0.1$: $e^{-0.987} \approx 0.373$ - already down to 37% of the initial peak.
Half-life of the amplitude: $t = \ln 2/\pi^2 \approx 0.0702$ time units; the mode $n=3$ decays $9$ times faster ($e^{-9\pi^2 t}$).

blocks.caption: The fundamental mode $\sin(\pi x)$ frozen at $t = 0$, $t \approx 0.1$ (factor $0.37$) and $t \approx 0.2$ (factor $0.14$): the shape never changes, only the amplitude melts away.

blocks.text: The explicit scheme: diffusion on a grid

blocks.md: Discretise space with step $\Delta x$ and time with step $\Delta t$, and replace $u_{xx}$ by the central second difference. This gives the **explicit scheme** $u_i^{\,n+1} = u_i^{\,n} + r\,(u_{i+1}^{\,n} - 2u_i^{\,n} + u_{i-1}^{\,n})$ with the mesh number $r = \alpha \Delta t/\Delta x^2$. Each new value is a weighted average of its neighbours, so the scheme *is* discrete diffusion, but it is only stable for $r \le 1/2$; beyond that, rounding noise amplifies and the solution oscillates itself to death.

blocks.title: Hand-verified scheme step
items: Rod $L = 1$, $\alpha = 1$: nodes at $x = 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1$ ($\Delta x = 0.25$), ends fixed at $0$.
Initial profile $u(x,0) = 100\,x(1-x)$, so interior values are $u_1 = 18.75$, $u_2 = 25.00$, $u_3 = 18.75$.

blocks.caption: The two hand steps above, reproduced exactly. Boundaries stay pinned; the centre cools from 25.00 to 22.50 to 20.00.

blocks.md: Sanity-check the scheme against the exact solution. The sine series of $100\,x(1-x)$ on $[0,1]$ is $\sum_{n \text{ odd}} \frac{800}{n^3\pi^3}\sin(n\pi x)$, whose centre value at $t = 0.025$ (two steps) is $\frac{800}{\pi^3}e^{-\pi^2 \times 0.025} - \frac{800}{27\pi^3}e^{-9\pi^2 \times 0.025} \approx 25.799 \times 0.7814 - 0.956 \times 0.1086 \approx 20.05$. The scheme's $20.00$ is within 0.3%, the discretisation error is doing exactly what theory predicts (a small undershoot, since diffusion has barely had time to act).

blocks.title: Halve $\Delta x$, quarter $\Delta t$
blocks.md: Because $r = \alpha\Delta t/\Delta x^2$, refining the grid by a factor of 2 forces $\Delta t$ down by a factor of **4** to keep $r \le 1/2$. The explicit scheme is cheap per step but step-hungry, the motivation for implicit and Crank-Nicolson methods, which cost more per step but take unconditional time steps (next lesson).

The Black-Scholes PDE $V_t + rS V_S + \tfrac12\sigma^2 S^2 V_{SS} - rV = 0$ is a heat equation wearing a suit. The change of variables $x = \ln(S/K)$, $\tau = \tfrac12\sigma^2(T - t)$ removes the first-order terms and rescales time, leaving $w_\tau = w_{xx} + (\text{lower-order terms})$ - the backward-in-time heat equation with a decay term. The $\tfrac12\sigma^2 S^2 V_{SS}$ term **is** the diffusion term: volatility is diffusivity for prices, which is why $\sigma^2$ multiplies the second derivative and why option values smooth out as time passes. Everything in this lesson, mode decay, stability limits, the maximum principle, transfers directly to the finite-difference pricing engines built in the following lessons.

blocks.title: Volatility is diffusivity
blocks.md: In the transformed Black-Scholes PDE the role of $\alpha$ is played by $\sigma^2/2$: doubling volatility doubles the diffusion speed, exactly as copper diffuses heat faster than steel. This is why far-from-expiry option prices depend so weakly on today's spot, diffusion has smeared the payoff's dependence across the whole log-price axis.

guidedExercise.prompt: A rod of length $L = 2$ has ends held at $0$ and initial profile $u(x,0) = 5\sin(\pi x/2)$, with $\alpha = 0.5$. (a) Write the exact solution. (b) Compute the amplitude factor at $t = 1$ (use $e^{-1.232} \approx 0.292$). (c) How many times faster does the $n = 2$ mode decay than the fundamental mode?
hints: Only one mode is present: $B_1$ times the exponential clock $e^{-\alpha(\pi/L)^2 t}$.
Compute the exponent $\alpha(\pi/L)^2 t$ with $L = 2$ before touching $e$.
The mode-$n$ decay rate is $\alpha(n\pi/L)^2$ - compare exponents.
guidedExercise.solution: (a) $u(x,t) = 5\,e^{-0.5(\pi/2)^2 t}\sin(\pi x/2) = 5\,e^{-1.2324\,t}\sin(\pi x/2)$. (b) At $t = 1$: $5 \times 0.292 \approx 1.46$, so the peak temperature has fallen from 5 to about 1.46. (c) Mode decay rates scale as $n^2$: the $n=2$ mode decays $2^2 = \mathbf{4}$ times faster than the fundamental mode.

independentExercise.prompt: On the grid of the lesson ($\Delta x = 0.25$, ends pinned at $0$, $\alpha = 1$), suppose the interior values at step $n$ are $u_1 = 14.25$, $u_2 = 20.0$, $u_3 = 14.25$. (a) With $\Delta t = 0.0125$ ($r = 0.2$), compute $u_1$ and $u_2$ at step $n+1$. (b) A colleague proposes $\Delta t = 0.05$ on the same grid. Compute the resulting $r$ and state whether the explicit scheme is stable, with justification. (c) What $\Delta t$ would keep $r \le 0.5$ if the grid were refined to $\Delta x = 0.125$?
hints: Apply the update $u_i^{\,n+1} = u_i^{\,n} + r(u_{i+1}^{\,n} - 2u_i^{\,n} + u_{i-1}^{\,n})$ with the pinned boundary $u_0 = 0$.
Refining $\Delta x$ by a factor of 2 shrinks the stable $\Delta t$ by a factor of 4.
independentExercise.solution: (a) $u_1^{\,n+1} = 14.25 + 0.2\,(20 - 28.5 + 0) = 14.25 - 1.7 = 12.55$. $u_2^{\,n+1} = 20 + 0.2\,(14.25 - 40 + 14.25) = 20 - 2.3 = 17.7$. (b) $r = 0.05/0.0625 = 0.8 > 0.5$: **unstable**, each step amplifies alternating components (the amplification factor $1 - 4r = -2.2$ lies outside $[-1,1]$), so oscillations blow up. (c) $\Delta x = 0.125$ gives $\Delta x^2 = 0.015625$, so $\Delta t \le 0.5 \times 0.015625 = 0.0078125$ - a quarter of the coarse grid's $0.0125$, as predicted.

commonMistakes: Forgetting the stability constraint: taking a large $\Delta t$ with the explicit scheme produces oscillating, exploding solutions that look like bugs but are pure $r > 1/2$.
Dropping the $\Delta x^2$ when forming $r = \alpha\Delta t/\Delta x^2$ - the mesh number scales with $\Delta x^2$, not $\Delta x$.
Assuming the heat equation can be run backward in time to recover an initial profile; it is ill-posed and amplifies noise catastrophically.
Believing interior maxima can appear spontaneously: the maximum principle forbids it, maxima live at $t = 0$ or on the boundary.
realWorldApplication: Heat and diffusion models govern heat-sink design in low-latency hardware, contaminant transport, and image-blurring algorithms; the explicit scheme above is the simplest instance of the time-stepping loops that run in every finite-difference solver.
quantFinanceApplication: The Black-Scholes PDE reduces to the heat equation under $x = \ln(S/K)$, $\tau = \tfrac12\sigma^2(T-t)$: volatility acts as diffusivity, and the explicit scheme's stability analysis reappears verbatim in the finite-difference pricers built in the next lessons (with the payoff as the 'initial' profile at expiry).
summary: The heat equation $u_t = \alpha u_{xx}$ says temperature rises where the profile sits below its neighbours' average; $\alpha$ sets the diffusion speed.
Separation of variables gives $u = \sum B_n e^{-\alpha(n\pi/L)^2 t}\sin(n\pi x/L)$: each mode decays exponentially, $n^2$ times faster for mode $n$.
Heat solutions smooth instantly, run backward only with catastrophic ill-posedness, and obey a maximum principle (interior maxima only at $t=0$ or the boundary).

The explicit scheme $u_i^{\,n+1} = u_i^{\,n} + r(u_{i+1}^{\,n} - 2u_i^{\,n} + u_{i-1}^{\,n})$ is stable only for $r = \alpha\Delta t/\Delta x^2 \le 1/2$; the lesson's verified grid produces centre values 25.00, 22.50, 20.00 against an exact 20.05.
Black-Scholes is a rescaled heat equation: $\tfrac12\sigma^2S^2V_{SS}$ is diffusion, $\sigma^2/2$ plays the role of $\alpha$.

quiz.prompt: For $u(x,t) = e^{-\pi^2 t}\sin(\pi x)$ on a unit rod, what is the amplitude factor at $t = 0.1$, to two decimal places?
quiz.explanation: $e^{-\pi^2 \times 0.1} = e^{-0.987} \approx 0.373$. The shape is unchanged; only the amplitude decays.

quiz.prompt: With $r = 0.2$, ends pinned at zero, and interior values $u_1 = 18.75$, $u_2 = 25$, $u_3 = 18.75$, what is $u_2$ after one explicit-scheme step?
The explicit scheme for the heat equation is stable when:
options: There is no condition, the explicit scheme is unconditionally stable
quiz.explanation: The amplification factor $1 - 4r\sin^2(k\Delta x/2)$ must stay in $[-1, 1]$, which requires $r \le 1/2$. Unconditional stability is the selling point of implicit methods, not the explicit one.

quiz.prompt: Select every statement that is true for solutions of the heat equation on a closed rod.
options: An interior maximum can only occur at $t = 0$
Solving backward in time is generally ill-posed
Solutions develop ever-sharper gradients over time
quiz.explanation: High-frequency modes decay fastest, so solutions smooth out (never sharpen); the maximum principle pins interior maxima to $t = 0$; backward evolution amplifies high-frequency noise without bound.

quiz.prompt: In the Black-Scholes PDE, which term plays the role of the heat equation's diffusion term $\alpha\,u_{xx}$?
quiz.explanation: The second-derivative term $\tfrac12\sigma^2S^2V_{SS}$ is diffusion, with effective diffusivity $\sigma^2/2$ after the log-price change of variables. $rSV_S$ is transport (drift), $-rV$ is the discounting sink.

quiz.prompt: Explain in one or two sentences why larger diffusivity $\alpha$ makes a rod cool faster, using the mode decomposition.
quiz.modelAnswer: Each mode decays like $e^{-\alpha(n\pi/L)^2t}$, so $\alpha$ multiplies every decay rate: larger $\alpha$ scales up all exponents, making every mode, and hence the whole profile, flatten faster.
quiz.explanation: The decay clock of every mode is $\alpha(n\pi/L)^2 t$; doubling $\alpha$ doubles all decay rates, exactly as doubling $\sigma^2$ speeds up the smearing of option payoffs.

flashcards.back: $u_t = \alpha\,u_{xx}$ on $0 < x < L$; $\alpha$ has units $\text{m}^2/\text{s}$ and sets the diffusion speed.
$u(x,t) = \sum_{n} B_n\, e^{-\alpha(n\pi/L)^2 t}\sin(n\pi x/L)$ - mode $n$ decays $n^2$ times faster than the fundamental mode.
$u_i^{\,n+1} = u_i^{\,n} + r(u_{i+1}^{\,n} - 2u_i^{\,n} + u_{i-1}^{\,n})$, $r = \alpha\Delta t/\Delta x^2$; stable iff $r \le 1/2$.
On a closed rod the maximum temperature occurs at $t = 0$ or at the boundary, the interior never spontaneously exceeds its neighbourhood.
With $x = \ln(S/K)$, $\tau = \tfrac12\sigma^2(T-t)$, the BS PDE becomes a backward heat equation; $\sigma^2/2$ plays the role of $\alpha$.
